newsitem.title: USA: UAW sets new strike deadline in American Axle talks.
newsitem.headline: UAW sets new strike deadline in American Axle talks.

text.p: United Auto Workers bargainers Sunday night issued a new strike threat for 7 a.m. EST Monday against a major auto supplier after a weekend of marathon negotiations failed to produce a new contract.
UAW President Stephen Yokich and UAW Vice President Richard Shoemaker said in a statement that talks with American Axle & Manufacturing Inc. would continue through Sunday evening.
A strike would force General Motors Corp. to suspend production at its 11 North American light truck plants within days.

"Despite intensive efforts this weekend, we have been unable to reach agreement with the company on satisfactory terms for our members," Yokich and Shoemaker said. "We underscore our commitment to reach a tentative agreement that maintains the wages, benefits and contractual rights that our members expect at this profitable manufacturer."
UAW members have remained on the job at American Axle and have not put up picket signs all weekend despite the expiration of the previous strike deadline at midnight Friday.
The two sides are attempting to hammer out a new three-year pact for 7,200 UAW members at five plants in Detroit, Three Rivers, Michigan, and Buffalo, New York.
A company spokesman could not be reached for comment.
American Axle supplies rear axles for GM's pickup trucks and sport utility vehicles, axles for the Camaro and Firebird rear-drive cars, as well as parts for other passenger cars.

Because of tight axle inventories industry-wide, GM would be forced to suspend production at its 11 North American light truck assembly plants within two days of a strike, analysts said. Such a shutdown would cost the world's largest automaker about $20 million in a day in lost profits, analysts said.

American Axle also makes axle shafts that Ford Motor Co. uses in its F-150 pickup trucks, Expedition and Explorer sport/utilities and some rear-drive passenger cars. It also makes axles for a small number of Chrysler Corp. light truck products.

Company and union officials began talking about 6 a.m. Friday and recessed early Saturday evening before resuming again Sunday morning. UAW leaders let a strike deadline expire at midnight Friday without any picketing action. No new deadline was set.
"The mood is still good. Progress is being made," said a person close to the talks who did not want his name used.
UAW members have continued to report for work and the company's normal weekend operations of limited production and maintenance have gone on uninterrupted.

The American Axle talks have drawn attention because they mark the first time a GM spin-off company has had to negotiate a new contract. When GM spun off the supplier in 1994, new management agreed to abide by the terms of the previous UAW contract, which expired in September 1996.
In the current talks, the UAW is trying to force the company to adopt the same pattern contract the Big Three automakers agreed to for about 400,000 UAW members last fall.

Automakers guaranteed jobs for 95 percent of their current workforce in a contract that provides $2,000 lump sum payments in the first year and wage hikes of 3 percent in the second and third years. The pact allows automakers to pay new hires at 70 percent of the starting base hourly wage of about $19.
The company claims the Big Three pattern would put it at a significant cost disadvantage with its competitors.
A UAW strike against Johnson Controls Inc., a key seat supplier for Ford, reached its 20th day Sunday with no settlement.
